newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish pound vulnerable to further attacks - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Irish pound vulnerable to further attacks - analysts.

text.p: The Irish pound halted its plunge on Thursday, clinging to support as fierce selling waned. But analysts said its predicament remained grim as it hung precariously, 15 pfennigs above the rate at which the market believes it will enter a single European currency.

The punt plummeted more than four pfennigs on Wednesday, coming under heavy speculative attack for the second time in three weeks because of a market conviction that it must fall against the German currency before economic and monetary union (EMU) in January 1999.
"The dilemma is clear," said Dublin's NCB Stockbrokers. "Either the Irish pound will have to revalue or it will ultimately have to fall to its present central parity of 2.41 marks."

The punt charged to the top of the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) grid in 1996, spurred by a resurgent sterling, and has remained there ever since, at times more than 10 percent above its central ERM rate of 2.41 marks.

But as the conviction has grown that ERM central rates will be the eventual conversion rates for EMU and that Ireland will be part of the single currency, the punt's position has looked increasingly precarious.

This dilemma provoked a furious trading session at the end of April when the punt dived seven pfennigs, and another bout of fierce selling pressure on Wednesday which knocked it more than four pfennigs lower.

"When the Irish pound climbs to 2.60 marks, which it did yesterday, then it stands out like a sore thumb to international investors. At that level they would regard it as a raging sell," said Colin Hunt, economist at Bank Of Ireland Group Treasury.

Dealers said Wednesday's tumble was prompted partly by comments from Goldman Sachs. The investment bank recommended selling punts and buying the Finnish markka, pointing out that if the punt was not revalued it would drop towards its central rate.

Market talk that a more detailed report on the issue, due shortly from Goldman Sachs economist Martin Brookes, would be particularly bearish on the punt was the catalyst for much of Wednesday's selling, dealers said.
The selling pushed the punt down from 2.60 marks to just above 2.55, although it recovered some ground on Thursday to stand at 2.5609 by 0920 GMT.
But analysts said its troubles were far from over.

"I don't think the pressure on the punt will go away," said Riada Stockbrokers chief economist Dan McLaughlin. "The fundamental problem is still there -- the perception is that at the start of 1999 the authorities want it at its central rate of 2.41."
NCB Stockbrokers said an implied forward rate of 2.41 marks in January 1999 would equate to a spot rate of 2.50 marks, still more than six pfennigs below the current level.
One solution to the punt's dilemma would be to revalue it at a higher rate within the ERM. But many economists have dismissed this.

"I doubt very much if the Irish authorities would ask for a revaluation," McLaughlin said. He added political pressure from exporters and farmers, who have complained bitterly about the punt's strength and welcomed its fall, would discourage the government from requesting a revaluation.

"Also it opens up a can of worms in relation to the rest of the ERM," McLaughlin said. "One of the things about EMU is that you are not supposed to devalue within two years prior to it, and technically everyone would be devaluing."

The currency turmoil three weeks ago forced the Central Bank of Ireland into a surprise half-point rate rise to 6.75 percent on May 1, to try to halt the punt's decline and combat its inflationary implications.
Economists were divided over whether the bank would have to raise rates again.

"We won't have a hike in rates unless we have such a wall of money coming at the currency that the Irish pound goes below 2.50 marks," Hunt said. "I don't see that happening in the near term so I don't think currency movements are going to elicit a monetary response."

But McLaughlin said another hike was possible. "The problem is that the trade-weighted index went down nearly two percent yesterday. If that continues, in other words if we're falling both against the mark and sterling, they may react," he said.
"Just to deal with the domestic inflationary implications, you wouldn't rule out another half point (rise) in official rates. But I think they might wait and see before they do anything."
Ireland goes to the polls on June 6 and many economists said a rate rise was unlikely during the election campaign.

"Apart altogether from the fact that raising rates last time has not prevented a re-run of Irish pound selling, one factor that would militate against the central bank raising rates again now is the political sensitivity of such an action in the middle of a general election campaign," NCB Stockbrokers said.
